lessons.title: Ottawa ankle rule
facts: After acute ankle injury, ankle radiography is indicated with malleolar-zone pain plus either posterior-edge/tip tenderness at the medial or lateral malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately after injury and at evaluation. A positive rule prompts imaging, not a fracture diagnosis.
gaps: Acute ankle injury only; assess eligibility and clinical red flags. Do not use a negative rule to exclude tendon injury or all occult injuries.

lessons.title: Ottawa foot rule
facts: After acute midfoot injury, foot radiography is indicated with midfoot-zone pain plus navicular tenderness, base-of-fifth-metatarsal tenderness, or inability to take four steps both immediately and at evaluation.
gaps: Use the foot rule for the midfoot zone, not the ankle rule. A negative result does not exclude every injury or override clinical red flags.

lessons.title: Ottawa knee rule
facts: For acute knee trauma, radiography is indicated by any: age at least 55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular-head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and at evaluation.
gaps: Acute trauma rule, not a chronic-knee-pain or ligament-injury rule. Do not silently replace AND with OR in the two weight-bearing time points.

lessons.title: Light’s criteria
facts: Pleural fluid is exudative if ANY is present: pleural/serum protein ratio >0.5; pleural/serum LDH ratio >0.6; pleural LDH > two-thirds the laboratory upper limit of normal serum LDH. The third criterion uses the serum reference limit, not the measured serum value.
gaps: Classification does not establish etiology. Diuresed heart failure may be misclassified; interpret with clinical context.

lessons.title: Wells PE score (two-level)
facts: PE Wells: DVT signs 3; PE more likely than alternative 3; heart rate >100 adds 1.5; immobilization >3 days or surgery in previous 4 weeks 1.5; prior DVT/PE 1.5; hemoptysis 1; malignancy treated within 6 months or palliative 1. More than 4 is PE likely; at most 4 is unlikely.
gaps: Pretest probability is not diagnosis. Follow the applicable imaging/D-dimer pathway; do not apply unmodified in pregnancy or an unstable patient.

lessons.title: Wells DVT score (two-level)
facts: DVT Wells: 1 each for active cancer, leg paralysis/paresis/recent cast, bed rest at least 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, deep-vein tenderness, entire-leg swelling, calf difference at least 3 cm, symptomatic-leg pitting edema, nonvaricose collateral veins, or prior DVT. Subtract 2 for an equally likely alternative. At least 2: likely; at most 1: unlikely.
gaps: Calf comparison location and the complete clinical pathway must be checked in the source; a score alone neither diagnoses nor excludes DVT.

lessons.title: PERC
facts: Only after establishing low clinical probability, PERC-negative requires all eight: age <50, pulse <100/min, room-air oxygen saturation at least 95%, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no recent surgery/trauma, no prior DVT/PE, and no exogenous estrogen.
gaps: Do not use in higher pretest probability, as a severity score, or as a general pregnancy rule. A positive criterion does not diagnose PE; it means this rule does not exclude PE. Exact recent-trauma definitions require the source.

lessons.title: CURB-65
facts: Adult CAP: 1 each for confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, respiratory rate at least 30/min, systolic BP <90 or diastolic BP at most 60 mmHg, and age at least 65. This estimates mortality risk and supports, but does not replace, disposition judgment.
gaps: Do not substitute BUN in mg/dL for urea in mmol/L without explicit conversion. Oxygenation, pregnancy, frailty and home support may change disposition. Exact risk/action bands require a scoped pathway.

facts: AKI is defined by serum creatinine rise at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours.

lessons.title: Diabetes diagnostic criteria
facts: Diabetes thresholds: A1c at least 6.5%, fasting plasma glucose at least 126 mg/dL, or 2-hour 75-g OGTT glucose at least 200 mg/dL; random glucose at least 200 mg/dL requires classic symptoms or hyperglycemic crisis. Confirm abnormal testing when hyperglycemia is not unequivocal.
gaps: A1c can be unreliable in altered red-cell turnover or hemoglobin variants; gestational testing uses different criteria.

facts: All three are needed: glucose at least 200 mg/dL OR diabetes history; beta-hydroxybutyrate at least 3 mmol/L OR urine ketones at least 2+; pH <7.3 OR bicarbonate <18 mmol/L.

lessons.title: Canadian CT Head Rule
facts: ACEP recommends the Canadian CT Head Rule as decision support in eligible adults with minor head injury. Apply its original inclusion/exclusion criteria; anticoagulant/antiplatelet use can limit safe rule-out.

For the CCHR version described in the original published abstract, five high-risk features are GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open skull fracture, basal skull-fracture signs, at least 2 vomiting episodes, or age at least 65. Two additional medium-risk features are pre-impact amnesia over 30 minutes or a dangerous mechanism. High-risk features target neurosurgical intervention; medium-risk features address clinically important brain injury.
gaps: Establish original minor-head-injury eligibility and exclusions before using a negative rule. Full dangerous-mechanism operational definitions are not loaded; do not infer a negative rule from an undefined mechanism. Do not extrapolate to children, anticoagulated patients or every head strike. The PubMed rendering of the abstract loses equality signs; the publisher abstract and ACEP 2023 clarify at least 2 episodes and at least 65 years.

lessons.title: New Orleans criteria
facts: ACEP identifies New Orleans criteria as an alternative adult minor-head-injury CT decision tool, with lower specificity than the Canadian CT Head Rule.

In the original eligible minor-head-injury population with GCS 15 and a normal brief neurologic examination after loss of consciousness, any of seven findings supports CT: headache, vomiting, age over 60, drug/alcohol intoxication, short-term memory deficit, trauma above the clavicles, or seizure.
gaps: Do not apply a negative rule outside original GCS/injury eligibility, to children, or to exclude CT in anticoagulated patients. A CT indication is not a diagnosis of intracranial injury.

lessons.title: Canadian C-spine rule
facts: The adult Canadian C-spine assessment is ordered: high-risk features (age at least 65, dangerous mechanism or limb paresthesias) lead to imaging without testing neck rotation. NICE examples of dangerous mechanism include a fall over 1 m or 5 steps, axial loading, high-speed collision, rollover/ejection, motorized recreation or bicycle/horse injury.

Only with no high-risk feature, look for a low-risk feature permitting safe range-of-motion assessment: minor rear-end collision, comfortable sitting, ambulatory since injury, absent midline tenderness or delayed neck pain. No low-risk feature supports imaging. When safe to assess, inability to actively rotate 45 degrees in both directions supports imaging.
gaps: Apply only to an alert, reliable appropriate trauma population; do not force movement or assess rotation before excluding high-risk features. NICE cautions that application to children is difficult. This is not an instruction to clear every patient with normal rotation.

lessons.title: PECARN pediatric head-injury pathways
facts: CDC recommends validated pediatric head-injury rules to guide imaging decisions; CT is not routinely used to diagnose pediatric mild TBI.

PECARN very-low-risk assessment separates children under 2 from those aged 2 and older after eligible minor blunt trauma (GCS 14-15, assessed within 24 hours). Under 2: normal mental status, no scalp hematoma except frontal, no loss of consciousness or less than 5 seconds, nonsevere mechanism, no palpable skull fracture, and normal behavior per parent. Age 2 and older: normal mental status, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, nonsevere mechanism, no basilar skull-fracture signs, and no severe headache.

Severe mechanism includes ejection/rollover or another passenger death, pedestrian or unhelmeted bicyclist struck by motor vehicle, high-impact head strike, or a fall over 0.9 m under age 2 and over 1.5 m in the older branch. Failing very-low-risk criteria does not automatically mandate CT; observation versus imaging depends on the complete branch and context.
gaps: This summarizes very-low-risk criteria, not every high/intermediate-risk action branch or exclusion. Infants under 3 months, suspected abuse, deterioration, bleeding disorders, shunts and unreliable assessment need particular consideration. Do not invent an individual risk percentage or force CT for every positive finding.

facts: STOP-BANG is a screening tool, not a diagnostic test. Adult OSA diagnosis relies on sleep testing interpreted with symptoms and clinical context.
gaps: Questionnaire items, point thresholds and reuse permissions are not reproduced here; use the original instrument. Do not infer OSA diagnosis from screening score alone.

lessons.title: McIsaac / modified Centor
facts: IDSA conditionally suggests a clinical score to help decide which patients aged at least 3 years with sore throat need GAS testing; a score estimates probability and does not itself confirm GAS or justify an invented antibiotic regimen. Consider testing high-risk patients even with a low score.

McIsaac adds one each for absent cough, tender swollen anterior cervical nodes, temperature over 38 C, and tonsillar swelling/exudate. The age modification adds 1 at ages 3-14 and 0 at 15-44; older age subtracts 1. IDSA Table 2 labels low 0-1, intermediate 2-3, high 4-5.
gaps: Age-45 boundary wording differs between the IDSA displayed table (>45) and AFP 2023 (45 and older). Do not assign an exact age-45 point from this summary; resolve against the selected validated version. Do not apply to children under 3 or replace testing/complication assessment with the score.

lessons.title: HEART chest-pain score
facts: HEART stratifies risk in adults with possible ACS in an emergency-department evaluation; its five domains are history, ECG, age, cardiac risk factors and troponin. Each contributes 0-2 points; the total spans 0-10. It does not establish ACS or evaluate every dangerous cause of chest pain.

Version pinned to the 2018 AFP table: history low/moderate/high suspicion gives 0/1/2; ECG normal/nonspecific repolarization/significant ST depression gives 0/1/2. Age at most 45 / over 45 but under 65 / at least 65 gives 0/1/2. No / 1-2 / at least 3 risk factors or atherosclerotic disease gives 0/1/2. Troponin at most the assay normal limit / over 1 but under 3 times / at least 3 times gives 0/1/2.

When all components are testable, sum E+V+M for a total 3-15, but report the individual responses and trends. If intubation, local injury, paralysis or another factor prevents assessment, record that component as not testable (NT); do not assign a false 1 or manufacture a numeric total.
gaps: This is standard GCS, not a full pediatric adaptation or GCS-P. Sedation, intoxication, language barriers and pre-existing impairment affect interpretation. A total alone does not identify the cause of impaired consciousness or dictate a universal airway/disposition action.
lessons.opening: I will describe a simulated patient. Identify the eye, verbal and motor responses one at a time, then give a total only if all three are testable. Explain your reasoning before I give feedback.
stages: Component reporting, total if testable, trends and limitations

practice_cases.presentation: Simulated adult: eyes open before you speak; speaks coherently but gives the wrong location/date; follows a two-part command. No interfering factors.
practice_cases.explanation: Spontaneous eye opening E4, confused coherent speech V4, obeying commands M6. Report E4 V4 M6, total 14.

practice_cases.presentation: Simulated adult: opens eyes only to pressure, makes only groaning sounds, and shows rapid normal flexion of the arm without localizing to the head/neck stimulus. No interfering factors.
practice_cases.explanation: Eye response to pressure E2, sounds V2, normal flexion M4: total 8. Normal flexion differs from localization and abnormal flexion.

practice_cases.presentation: Simulated adult: endotracheal tube prevents speech; opens eyes to sound and follows a two-part command. Eye and motor responses are otherwise testable.
practice_cases.explanation: Report E3 VNT M6 and the intubation limitation. Do not substitute V1 or manufacture a total.
